chief_complaint: angina on minimal exertion, diabetes, and abnormal stress test
hpi_details: A 58-year-old male presents to the clinic with angina on minimal exertion, diabetes, and abnormal stress test. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his blood sugar spikes from his diabetes are straining his heart muscle and irritating the nerves in his chest.
concerns: He is worried he will need open-heart bypass surgery and be left unable to manage his small business and provide for his family.
expectations: He hopes to be prescribed a daily heart pill or patch that prevents the chest ache so he can avoid surgery altogether.

available_results.value: Large reversible perfusion defects in the anterior and inferior walls with 2.5 mm exercise-induced ST depression

investigation_events.title: Coronary angiography
investigation_events.availability_message: The coronary angiography report is now available.

results.value: 85% proximal LAD, 80% circumflex, and 90% right coronary artery stenoses; SYNTAX score 35

clinical_knowledge.topic: Suspected Multivessel Coronary Artery Disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Three-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes coronary angiography to define anatomy, followed by individualized medical and revascularization planning, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: angina on minimal exertion, diabetes, and abnormal stress test

Key HPI features: A 58-year-old male presents to the clinic with angina on minimal exertion, diabetes, and abnormal stress test. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Three-Vessel CAD.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Three-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Single-vessel disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rest pain — unstable angina.
management_principles: Plan for suspected multivessel CAD: coronary angiography to define anatomy, followed by multidisciplinary revascularization planning when indicated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI Guideline for Coronary Artery Revascularization

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of angina on minimal exertion, diabetes, and abnormal stress test. HPI: severe coronary atherosclerosis.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Three-Vessel CAD.
reference_soap.assessment: High-risk coronary artery disease is suspected, but the extent of coronary disease requires angiographic definition.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for suspected multivessel CAD: coronary angiography to define anatomy, followed by multidisciplinary revascularization planning when indicated. CABG is often favored for diabetes with complex multivessel disease, but the choice between medical therapy, PCI, and CABG depends on anatomy, ventricular function, comorbidity, and patient preference. Seek urgent assessment for rest pain or worsening symptoms. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Three-Vessel CAD
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Three-Vessel CAD
Implement evidence-based management plan: Coronary angiography, refer for bypass surgery (CABG)

teaching.one_liner: Severe atherosclerotic narrowing of all three major coronary arteries, causing angina on minimal exertion — typically managed with bypass surgery given the extent of disease.

must_ask.say: How little activity brings on the chest pain now?
Has anyone told you about your stress test results?
Have you had a stent before?
How far can you walk before the pain starts?

history.answer: Doctor, I have been getting chest pain even with very light physical activity, and it has been getting worse over the past few weeks.
It started about a month ago when walking up a small hill, but recently it happens even when I just walk slowly across a room.
It is right in the center of my chest, behind the breastbone, covering an area about the size of my fist.
It feels like a heavy squeezing pressure or tight band across my chest, not sharp or stabbing.
Yes, when it gets strong, the tightness spreads up into my lower jaw and down my left shoulder and arm.
Each episode lasts about five to ten minutes and subsides when I rest. It happens three or four times every day now.
At its worst, I would rate it around 6 out of 10. The intensity and frequency have both steadily increased over the past month.
Walking or carrying light groceries brings it on, and sitting quietly relieves it within minutes. It has not happened while I am resting in bed or sleeping.
Taking a deep breath, coughing, or changing my body position does not change the pain at all, and pressing on my ribs does not hurt.
No, eating has no effect on it, and I do not have acid reflux, indigestion, or pain when swallowing.
I get slightly short of breath and break into a mild cold sweat when the tightness occurs, and I have felt unusually tired lately. I have not had any nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, cough, or phlegm.
No, I have not had a cold, the flu, or any viral illness recently.
No, neither leg is swollen or painful, and I have not had any recent surgeries, prolonged bed rest, or long flights.
No, there are no rashes, blisters, or redness anywhere on my skin.
I feel anxious because of these symptoms, but I do not have sudden panic attacks, a sense of doom out of nowhere, or numbness in my fingers.
No, I have not had any injuries to my chest, and I haven't done any heavy lifting or unusual upper-body strain.
My primary doctor had me take a treadmill exercise test last week and said it was definitely abnormal with signs of poor blood supply, so they sent me here right away.
Right now, I can barely walk half a block on flat ground or climb half a flight of stairs before the tightness forces me to stop.
No, I have never had a heart attack, an angiogram, or stents placed before.
I have had type 2 diabetes for about seven years. I take my pill every day and my blood sugar usually stays fairly controlled.
My blood pressure and cholesterol have been slightly high before, but my doctor told me the diabetes is my biggest risk factor.
Other than diabetes, I do not have any other chronic medical conditions.
I had my appendix removed when I was in college, but I have never been hospitalized since then.
I take metformin 500 milligrams twice a day for my diabetes. I don't take any other prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or contrast dye.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife. My work is mostly at a desk, so this fatigue and chest tightness are really affecting me.
My father suffered a heart attack in his early sixties, and my mother had high blood pressure.

I thought my diabetes might be acting up and putting extra strain on my heart and the nerves in my chest. I'm terrified this will lead to open-heart surgery and put me out of commission so I can't run my business or support my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 132/84 mmHg in both arms, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and body temperature is 36.7°C.
The patient is an alert, comfortable-appearing male in no acute distress, with no diaphoresis, pallor, or respiratory distress.
No rashes, vesicular eruptions, or lesions on the anterior chest wall or back.
Normal jugular venous pressure without distension or abnormal pulsations.
No chest wall deformity, and no tenderness or reproduction of pain upon palpation of the ribs or costochondral junctions.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no heart murmurs, S3, S4, or pericardial friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout with no hepatosplenomegaly or epigastric tenderness.
No peripheral pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.
Calves are symmetric, non-tender, and without swelling, erythema, or cord-like induration.
Radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are intact, 2+ and symmetric bilaterally.
